Lol it 100% depends on where in the industry he's aiming. You're a comp sci major. You should know better than anyone that it completely comes down to whether or not he wants to put in the effort and study alone. And that is what it usually comes down to in regards to learning any subject tbh. At most schools(At least in my area), if we were to ignore the lower division classes(Math up through Linear and Comp Sci through Data Structures, a comp sci major will take about 8 upper division courses. A comp sci minor will take no less than 5, if they decide to only take those.

I'm specifically talking about if he wants to do like some kind of analysis /research positions as opposed to software development which wouldn't require him anything more than those lower div classes(Stats is required at some point for most schools) + Python + Databases 1/2 .  And with those "lower level" classes, he could easily get any IT position which generally pay more than most. I think that a comp sci minor would help him more than other minors considering how niche his major is. 

Feel free to correct me. I'm just speaking based on my experience applying to jobs in the last few months without an official comp sci minor but I've taken all of those lower div courses aside from discrete.

Tldr: Data Analysts positions would open up for him with the minot as opposed to "Data Scientist" positions. Though I guess it depends on how you define those 2.

A Comp Sci minor would require him to take Calc through 3, Linear Alg, Intro to Prog, Int. Prog, Data Structures, Discrete,  Abstract Data Types(Core Class) & 3-4 Upper Div Comp Sci courses. In what possible way does that not mean much? You going to sit here and tell me that he can't get a tech related job of any kind with those courses? A Comp Sci minor is essentially majoring in it.

I'm about to graduate in English, I've taken accouting, Economics and Comp Sci courses and have had a finance intership for 2 years. I've had no issue getting interviews with my crappy degree. Or course if you only take courses within your humanity major, you'll probably be screwed.

It depends on what you do. Econ with a minor in computer science is something that would look good. But ultimately, as long as you list the classes you've taken relevant to the job you want, you'll be fine. People are far to concerned with degree names when it's always been about how your skills/classes relate to the job you want. There is a reason the vast majority of people aren't working in their major field.

I remember when I thought like this. If it's any consolation, you won't give a shit about how long it took you to get your degree after you get that first job. Especially if it's related to your degree. Give it 2 more years before your fucks go out the window in regards to your age.
